verdicts.question: Did the Finance Act 2026 enact the 2% income-tax TCS on the sale of scrap (up from 1%)? Which sellers are covered (turnover thresholds), and does the exemption for buyers who use scrap in manufacturing survive under the Income-tax Act 2025? Which section carries it now?
verdicts.problems: No source could be checked: every page fetch on this machine is refused (proxy 403) and the session's WebSearch budget was already exhausted, so not one of the nine cited sources was found by snippet. The key claim, that the Finance Act 2026 (No. 4 of 2026, assent 30 March 2026, Gazette 271439, section 85) enacted the 2% rate, is unsupported by anything I could reach: the repository's own legal.md and industry-integration.md briefs, written the same day (29 Sept 2026), only cite the Budget 2026-27 memorandum (indiabudget.gov.in/doc/memo.pdf) for a PROPOSAL to raise TCS on scrap from 1% to 2% and expressly leave enactment as an open question; payments-and-finance.md likewise says '2% (proposed from 1 Apr 2026)'. The Act number, assent date, gazette file number, section 85, 'Sl. No. 4' in the section 394(1) Table, and the 'Form 127 / Rule 212 of the Income-tax Rules 2026' form number are all not confirmed by snippet and could be fabricated detail; they must be read from the gazette before being hard-coded. Claims that ARE consistent with the 1961-Act text carried into the 2025 Act (seller definition with the Rs 1 crore business / Rs 50 lakh profession test for individuals and HUFs; buyer exclusions; the manufacturing/processing declaration in duplicate with a copy to the Commissioner by the 7th of the next month; scrap definition unchanged) are plausible but also not confirmed by snippet. One substantive gap: section 394 TCS (old 206C(1)) is not displaced by buyer-side TDS on purchase of goods (old 194Q, now in s.393); the answer leaves this to the CA, but the default should be stated. Against the refined chain the model is incomplete: it flags TCS per material, but the definition turns on origin and lot type, so the flag must also depend on whether the lot is post-consumer (S0-S3 from households), a pre-processor's main output (S4-S9 flake, granule, ingot, crumb: a product, not scrap), or a pre-processor's residual/by-product lot or an industrial by-product listing (turnings, dross, slag, offcuts: scrap from manufacture or mechanical working, squarely in scope when the seller is a firm or company). Pre-processors and compounders qualify to give the manufacturing/processing declaration because 'processing' is in the exemption text, which the answer does not say.
verdicts.correction: Partly settled; enactment must be confirmed from the gazette before 13 October 2026. What is corroborated: Budget 2026-27 (Finance Bill 2026, 1 February 2026) proposed raising income-tax TCS on the sale of scrap from 1% to 2% with effect from 1 April 2026 (memorandum at indiabudget.gov.in/doc/memo.pdf, cited independently by the legal and industry-integration briefs). What is not yet confirmed from any page opened or snippet read: that the Finance Act 2026 carried the clause unchanged, its section number, its assent date and gazette copy, and the serial number of 'scrap' in the section 394(1) Table. Under the Income-tax Act 2025 (assent 21 August 2025, in force 1 April 2026, when the 1961 Act was repealed) TCS on specified goods sits in section 394, with 'buyer', 'scrap' and 'seller' defined in section 402; the definitions are carried over from the 206C Explanation: a 'seller' is the Government, a local authority, a statutory corporation, a company, a firm or a co-operative society, and an individual or HUF only if business turnover exceeded Rs 1 crore (Rs 50 lakh for a profession) in the preceding year, so a sole-proprietor kabadiwala under Rs 1 crore collects nothing while a yard, pre-processor or recycler that is a firm or company always is a seller. The exemption survives in substance: no TCS from a resident buyer who gives a written declaration (in duplicate, copy to the tax authority by the 7th of the following month) that the goods are for manufacturing, processing or producing articles or for generating power and not for trading; the buyer's PAN is required. Because 'processing' is in the text, pre-processors and compounders can give the declaration, not only manufacturers. The form's number under the Income-tax Rules 2026 is not confirmed; until the CA confirms it, store the declaration as a dated PDF plus PAN per buyer. Interaction: buyer-side TDS on purchase of goods (s.393, successor to 194Q) does not apply to a transaction on which TCS is collectible under section 394, so where TCS applies it prevails; the TCS base (GST-inclusive or not) stays a CA question. Refined-chain rule for the rulebook: TCS flag = seller is a 'seller' AND lot is 'scrap' AND no valid declaration on file, where 'scrap' is decided per lot type, not per material: post-consumer S0-S3 lots default OFF (see question 2); pre-processor main outputs S4-S9 (flake, granule, pulp, ingot, crumb, compound) OFF because they are products; pre-processor residual and by-product lots and industrial by-product listings from manufacture or mechanical working (turnings, dross, slag, offcuts, punchings) default ON. Rate: keep as a dated rulebook value, default 2% from 1 April 2026 pending gazette confirmation, with 1% as the fallback if the Finance Act did not carry the clause. Status: partly. Who to ask: the CA to read the Finance Act 2026 text and Income-tax Rules 2026 (section number, table serial, declaration form number, TCS base) and to confirm the s.393/s.394 precedence.

verdicts.question: Does the Act's definition of 'scrap' cover post-consumer recyclables that yards sell, such as newspaper, PET bottles and cartons?
verdicts.problems: None of the seven cited sources could be found by snippet (no search or fetch possible on this machine), so the case citations, appeal numbers and dates (Priya Blue Industries Tax Appeal 604 of 2015, 3 Nov 2015; Dhasawala Traders 1 Sept 2016; Lala Bharat Lal & Sons ITA 14-16/LKW/2019, 19 Feb 2020; Bharti Auto Products (2013) 145 ITD 1; Adisankara Spinning Mills 2010) are not confirmed by snippet. The legal substance is consistent with what is well known: the definition (origin in manufacture or mechanical working, plus not usable as such) is carried over verbatim into the 2025 Act; the Gujarat High Court in Priya Blue and later ITAT benches read both limbs strictly, while the Rajkot Special Bench in Bharti Auto Products held traders liable regardless of source; no CBDT circular resolves post-consumer material. The answer does not hold as written because its decision rule is too coarse for the refined chain: it decides by material family (paper/PET/glass/rags out, metal maybe in), whereas the definition decides by origin and lot type. Under the 30 Sept 2026 model, a pre-processor's residual waste and saleable by-product lots (each a separate lot with a yield) and the 400-plus industrial by-product listings (turnings, dross, slag, offcuts, foundry sand) arise precisely 'from the manufacture or mechanical working of materials' and are the clearest in-scope items, while a pre-processor's main outputs (S4-S9 flake, granule, ingot, crumb, compound) are products usable as such and outside the definition. The answer says nothing about either. Also note that Bharti Auto Products and a later Gujarat line (Navine Fluorine, Nathulal Lavti) mean a yard or pre-processor selling metal to a manufacturer cannot rely on the 'trader' argument alone; collecting the manufacturing/processing declaration remains the only safe neutraliser.
verdicts.correction: Probably not for household material, but the test is origin and usability, not material family. Section 402 of the Income-tax Act 2025 keeps the 1961 wording: scrap is 'waste and scrap from the manufacture or mechanical working of materials which is definitely not usable as such because of breakage, cutting up, wear and other reasons'. Old newspapers, PET bottles, cartons, glass bottles and rags collected from households (S0-S3 in the chain) come from consumption, not from a manufacturing process, and are bought because they are usable as raw material, so on the plain words they fall outside; the Gujarat High Court in CIT v. Priya Blue Industries and later ITAT benches (Lucknow, Ahmedabad) read the definition that way, while the Rajkot Special Bench in Bharti Auto Products held traders liable regardless of source, and no CBDT circular settles post-consumer material (citations, appeal numbers and dates could not be confirmed from any snippet and should be re-checked by counsel). Apply the definition per lot type across the refined chain: (a) post-consumer lots S0-S3 sold by kabadiwalas and yards: default outside scrap, no TCS, subject to counsel; (b) metal lots sold by yards: often mixed with industrial offcuts and turnings, so treat as potentially in scope and neutralise with the buyer's manufacturing/processing declaration; (c) pre-processor main outputs S4-S9 (PET flake, granules, copper from cable granulation, rubber crumb, ingots, pulp, compound): products usable as such, outside the definition; (d) pre-processor residual and by-product lots, and industrial by-product listings such as turnings, dross, slag, offcuts, punchings and foundry sand: squarely 'from manufacture or mechanical working', in scope whenever the seller is a firm, company or an individual over Rs 1 crore, unless the buyer gives the declaration; whether by-products that are used as-is (fly ash, bagasse, husk, whey) are 'not usable as such' is unsettled and is a counsel item. Decision: store 'scrap for TCS' as a per-lot-type flag with defaults as above, collect the processing/manufacturing declaration from every pre-processor, recycler, compounder and manufacturer buyer at onboarding, and obtain a written opinion from tax counsel before the first yard-to-pre-processor metal sale and before listing industrial by-products. Status: needs-pilot-or-counsel. Who to ask: tax counsel (section 402 definition applied to post-consumer lots, pre-processor residuals and industrial by-products), then the CA to set the flags.

verdicts.question: After the GST rate changes of 22 September 2025 (Notification 9/2025-CT(Rate)), which GST rate and HSN code apply to each material family: waste paper (4707), plastic scrap (3915), ferrous scrap (7204), copper/aluminium/brass scrap (7404/7602), glass cullet (7001), rags (6309/6310), e-waste (8549), batteries? Which value threshold applies to the 2% GST TDS on metal scrap under Notification 25/2024?
verdicts.problems: No snippet could be read (fetches refused, search budget exhausted), so nothing here is confirmed by snippet directly. The sources were, however, found independently: the same official copies are cited in four other repository documents written 29-30 Sept 2026 (gstcouncil.gov.in copies of Notification 06/2024-CT(Rate) and 25/2024-Central Tax, the CBIC section 51 page, the GSTN REG-07 advisory of 22 Oct 2024, and a CBIC copy of Notification 9/2025-CT(Rate)), and those documents state the same rates: 4707 and 7001 at 5%; 3915, 7204 and 7602 at 18%; 18% reverse charge on metal scrap from unregistered sellers from 10 Oct 2024; 2% GST TDS on registered-to-registered metal scrap over Rs 2.5 lakh per contract, ex-GST, same State. The founder's own plan states 5% for paper, glass cullet and rags and 18% for plastics, metal scrap, e-waste and batteries from the gazette copy. The rate history (plastic 3915 cut to 5% on 13 Oct 2017 and restored to 18% from 1 Oct 2021; e-waste 8549 raised to 18% from 18 July 2022; batteries 8507 uniformly 18% from 22 Sept 2025) and the section 51 mechanics match the law as known. Unconfirmed detail that should not be hard-coded from this answer: the schedule serial numbers (Sl. 317, 406, 391, 116, 263, 309, 331, 521, 480, 479) and the entry numbers 187A/101A/371A in the older notifications; the G.S.R. 629(E) number; and the 'spent batteries classified under 8549' statement (no source in the answer). Minor: Notification 06/2024-CT(Rate) is dated 8 October 2024 (the answer's source is dated 9 Oct). Arithmetic (2.5% CGST = 5%; 9% = 18%; 1%+1% = 2%) is right. No later development could be checked as of 30 Sept 2026, so treat the rates as current only until the CA confirms. Refined-chain gap: the table covers only S0-S3 scrap headings; it has no rows for pre-processor outputs (PET flake, plastic granules, cable-recovered copper, rubber crumb, pyrolysis oil, ingots, recovered pulp, re-refined oil), for compounds, or for industrial by-products (fly ash, slag, dross, bagasse, husk), and PET flake classification (3915 as scrap vs 3907 as polymer) has conflicting advance rulings, so those rows are open items for the CA rather than figures. Also state explicitly that the metal-scrap reverse charge and 2% GST TDS follow the 'metal scrap' heading: a baled or shredded/stripped metal lot (S3-S4) still under 7204/7404/7602 stays in scope, while an ingot (S7, headings 7206/7403/7601/7801) is not 'scrap' and drops out of both rules.
